authoritative_key.why_this_is_the_key: The commit the sweep recorded, not the version string and not the commit the tag points at. benchmarks/compare/results.json now writes its own identity, and its identity.git_commit field reads ad9158289df2e98a8bb4cf3deb7e189207d0d754; it also records that the working tree was dirty, which is stated rather than hidden. That commit is FIFTEEN COMMITS PAST the v2.0.0 tag, so -- exactly as with 1.1.0 -- the sweep did not run under the tag. What separates this entry from 1.1.0's is what fills the gap, and it was measured: git rev-list --count v2.0.0..ad91582 gives 15, and git diff --name-only v2.0.0 ad91582 -- src/ is EMPTY. The fifteen commits touch .github/workflows/, VERSIONING.md, benchmarks/history/, pyproject.toml, tests/unit/test_version.py and tools/mutation.py -- CI configuration, documentation and test tooling -- and no file under src/ at all. The one line they change outside documentation is a classifier in pyproject.toml, Development Status 4 - Beta to 5 - Production/Stable, which is upload metadata the extractor never reads. Both trees report __version__ 2.0.0. So the code this sweep measured is byte-identical to the v2.0.0 tag's extraction code, which is a stronger claim than 1.1.0 can make: there the six intervening commits were src/ work under an unbumped version string. The commit, not the version, is still the key -- it is quoted because it is what results.json says, and a reader can run the two commands above rather than take the label on trust.

what_was_measured_and_when: One full sweep, on an idle development machine, recorded into benchmarks/compare/results.json on 2026-10-04 with the runner's own identity block: three sizes (100 MB, 1 GB, 4 GB) over four implementations (gigaxml, raw_lxml, xmltodict, pandas), five repeats each, on freshly generated documents. This is the record 2.0.0rc4.json's what_would_close_this asked for -- an idle machine and regenerated data -- and it is why this entry is recorded: true where its four candidate predecessors are not. Each candidate left a residue (a build that failed, a Release job that died, a binary naming the wrong version, a version not yet published) and none of them was a sweep; this is a sweep, at a commit whose extraction code equals the tag's.
the_deciding_evidence_that_the_flagged_p: The comparison table's own guard, benchmarks/compare/verify_peaks.py, is STILL RED (rc=1) against this freshly re-recorded file, deliberately. It flags 15 of the 55 readings it checked, every one of them raw_lxml. The previous sweep flagged 10 of 60; the count moved for two reasons that point the same way: the fresh readings came out lower (23.4-24.6 MiB against 24.7-26.2 before), so the 1 GB group joined the 100 MB and 4 GB groups inside the band, and only 55 not 60 readings were checked, because pandas at 1 GB and 4 GB wrote peak_rss_mb: null five times each and are skipped rather than judged. That the flag is not a failure is now proven, not asserted. The decisive experiment varied the payload WITHIN a single record instead of across the document: two documents, the SAME 2,000 records, one carrying about 50 bytes per name element and one about 1 MiB -- a 5,000-fold difference in total document length. raw_lxml's peak moved from 23.0 to 25.8 MiB, +2.8 MiB. A thousandfold rise in the size of one record produced a 2.8 MiB rise in the peak, because a streaming parser holds one record at a time and releases it with clear() plus unlink before the next is parsed: the peak is the interpreter plus one record, and the document's total length does not enter it. If the sampler were dead -- a wrapper whose extraction ran in a grandchild, the failure verify_peaks.py exists to catch -- the payload would not reach the peak at all. It does, so the reading comes from the process that did the work. The contrast with a non-streaming reader is the definition of the word: xmltodict moves 40, then 189, then 705 MiB across the three document sizes because it holds the whole document; raw_lxml's ~24 MiB does not move with the document size because it does not.
the_guard_is_red_on_purpose_and_was_not_: verify_peaks.py has not been changed and its threshold MIN_MEANINGFUL_GAP_MIB has not been raised, and must not be: raising it would make the guard blind to the very class of streaming implementations it exists to protect. What the guard is missing is a second axis, and the evidence for it is already in results.json and thrown away. The guard reads only peak_rss_mb; the runner also records exit_code, rows_written and rows_in_document, and a flagged reading whose run wrote the full document (rows_written == rows_in_document) demonstrably did the work. The intended repair, judged here and implemented in a later task, is to split the guard into two verdicts: a reading BELOW the idle floor stays a hard failure, because it is physically impossible and means the sampler is broken; a reading merely WITHIN the band, when the same run wrote every row, is downgraded to a notice, because near-floor is what a correct bounded streaming parser is supposed to look like. Until that second axis is added the guard is red on unchanged code and stays out of CI, which is the honest state rather than a threshold moved to make the light green.
what_would_close_this: Nothing on the comparison side -- the sweep has been run and the figures above are that run's. Two things remain open, stated so neither is mistaken for done. First, benchmarks/perf-baseline.json was NOT re-recorded, and by its own measured_on note it cannot be from here: recorded in CI, not on a development machine, because the check it feeds runs on the shared ubuntu-latest runner and a reference taken from a desktop asserted a 42,246 rec/s floor on a runner that sustains 19,312, which goes red on unchanged code. That half must be re-recorded inside the CI job with --update, and until then 2.0.0's throughput is known on this machine while its CI baseline is still 1.1.0's. Second, verify_peaks.py is still rc=1 for the reason above; closing it means giving the guard its second axis, not re-measuring raw_lxml a fourth time, because the readings are correct and a re-measurement produces the same ~24 MiB. What would NOT close it: raising MIN_MEANINGFUL_GAP_MIB. The sentence that stood here before, that a sweep at 2.0.0 had not been run and that eleven of sixty readings sat inside the noise band, was true when written and is now false in both halves: the sweep has been run, and the count is 15 of 55. It is replaced rather than edited in place so the correction is visible.
no_numbers_were_fabricated_here: Every figure in this entry is copied from benchmarks/compare/results.json, which run_comparison.py wrote on 2026-10-04, and the walker tests/integration/test_benchmark_provenance.py recomputes each summary from its own per-run values. This key used to say the file was deliberately empty of numbers because nothing had been measured; that is no longer the state. What is unchanged is the rule: no number here describes a run that did not happen. The two pandas points at 1 GB and 4 GB carry nulls because every repeat failed (1 GB with an lxml encoding error, 4 GB because a memory-safety watchdog killed the child before the machine could swap itself to death); null is what those failures are -- not a zero, and not a borrowed number from another size.
this_is_the_first_version_actually_publi: Every earlier tag in this repository was built and, for the nine before the candidates, released as a GitHub Release; none of them reached an index. package.yml's pypi-publish job is gated on if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') && !contains(github.ref_name, 'rc'), so all four candidates -- whose names all contain 'rc' -- skipped it, and the tag-to-index path had never been walked until this tag. At v2.0.0 the guard does not fire: the name carries no 'rc', the job ran, and the package was published. That is the one fact this entry records that no earlier candidate could: 2.0.0 is the first version in this repository that a person can install from an index rather than download from a Release page or build from the tree, and the number a PyPI consumer sees is 2.0.0. A published version can be yanked from PyPI but not deleted, so this release is also the first whose tag cannot be re-cut to fix a defect in what it ships -- a repair would have to be a new version.
what_each_candidate_exposed_before_this_: The four candidates were not four attempts at one thing; each rehearsed the pipeline and each exposed a different defect, and this release is the first that is not spent on any of them. rc1 died before its build produced anything: packaging/gigaxml.spec reduced the version by asking int() of each dot-separated part, and the third part of 2.0.0rc1 is '0rc1', so all three platforms failed with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '0rc1' and no artifact existed. rc2 built on all three platforms and uploaded an artifact from each, and its release job -- assembly, SBOM, checksums, the Release page -- died on ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml', because that job declared an interpreter and no dependencies while importing tools/release_checksums.py; the tag therefore had artifacts and no Release page. rc3 built and assembled a Release page for the first time, and shipped a binary reporting the wrong version: a build reads its version from pyproject.toml and not from the tag, and the tree was not bumped when the tag was cut, so the tag and the page announced 2.0.0rc3 while the binary inside them announced 2.0.0rc2 -- which the tag guard added for rc2 caught, on its own releaser, the first time it ran. rc4 was the first candidate whose tree and tag named the same version, and it built, released and (like rc1 through rc3) skipped PyPI for its name. 2.0.0 is the first tag that is not a rehearsal: it carries no rc suffix, so it both skipped none of the pipeline and walked the publish step the four candidates never reached.
the_pipeline_had_never_run_on_a_pre_rele: The defect rc1 exposed had been present in the packaging spec since before any of this, and nine earlier tag builds went green with it. They went green because none of them was built from a tree that carried a pre-release suffix in the version the build reads: v0.9.0rc1 and v0.9.0rc2 were cut from a tree whose pyproject.toml read 0.9.0, and v1.2.0rc1 and v1.2.0rc2 from one that read 1.2.0. A tag named for a pre-release is not a tree that carries one, so four of the nine green builds were named with an 'rc' and taught the reduction nothing -- int(part) had never been handed a non-digit. The same shape repeats one level up in the publish gate: this workflow had never run on a tag whose name contained 'rc' against a tree whose version contained one, and the four candidates are the first versions where the tag, the tree and the publish condition were all exercised together. 2.0.0 is the first to pass that gate rather than be skipped by it.
the_classifier_shipped_to_pypi_was_beta: Read from the index, not from this tree: pip and the PyPI page both report 2.0.0 carrying 'Development Status :: 4 - Beta' and 'Typing :: Typed', with requires-python <3.14,>=3.11, while the pyproject.toml in this repository reads 'Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable'. The two are not the same build and the difference is one of order rather than of content: the classifiers are baked into the uploaded distribution metadata at publish time, and this repository's pyproject.toml did not carry the 5 - Production/Stable line until commit fb0f408, whose commit date is later on the same day than the creation date of the v2.0.0 tag, which is 8aee010f0696f04881fcc0f6695a81b1f74c116f. So the tag was cut and published from a tree whose classifier still said Beta, and the hand edit that made the tree say Production/Stable landed after the artefact that carries the old value had already been uploaded. The mismatch cannot be repaired by re-uploading: PyPI refuses to reuse a version number, and 2.0.0 is now the name of an artefact that is already on the index, so the repository and the page will disagree about this version until the next 2.0.x that actually changes something carries the correct classifier forward. The order lesson is the part worth keeping, and it is the reverse of how the plan for this release read: 'restore 5 - Production/Stable once 2.0 passes the release gate' was read as meaning after the tag, and it has to mean before the tag. A classifier is a field of the build, not a note about the build, so it is fixed at upload and a later edit to the tree only changes the tree. The review step that made the edit was right about the value and wrong about when it could still reach anything.
